title: The demand for human enhancement technologies - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A new NBER working paper based on a 5,556-person U.S. survey experiment finds about 53% would adopt human enhancement technologies, that framing a technology as enhancing rather than restorative cuts adoption by roughly five percentage points (as much as a severe side-effect profile), and that productivity enhancement draws the most ethical concern yet the least demanded regulation. Tyler Cowen amplifies the productivity finding and calls the authors' policy conclusion 'completely unwarranted' and a classic case of underidentified political bias in academic reasoning.

insights.claim: In a nationally representative U.S. survey experiment with 5,556 respondents on human enhancement technologies, about 53% said they would adopt.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A roughly even split means enhancement products face no majority veto in the U.S. market but also no consensus mandate — segmentation, not mass launch, is the go-to-market.
insights.locator: We examine this using a nationally representative U.S. survey experiment

insights.claim: About 28% of respondents said they would not adopt a human enhancement technology at any level of benefit, a refusal driven overwhelmingly by the enhancing framing rather than by risk, consistent with a non-compensatory constraint for a substantial subgroup.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A hard floor of roughly a quarter of the population cannot be converted by improving efficacy or safety — TAM models that assume price/benefit elasticity will overstate penetration.
insights.quote: About 28% would not adopt at any benefit.
insights.locator: About 28% would not adopt at any benefit

insights.claim: Describing a technology as enhancing rather than restorative lowers stated adoption by about five percentage points — the same magnitude of deterrence as attaching a severe side-effect profile.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Positioning language is worth as much as clinical safety data for enhancement-adjacent products; expect companies to market therapeutically even when the use case is elective.
insights.quote: Framing the technology as enhancing rather than restorative lowers adoption by about five percentage points, as much as a severe side-effect profile.
insights.locator: Framing the technology as enhancing rather than restorative

insights.claim: Most respondents who would adopt a human enhancement technology still favor strict regulation of it, and most who would never adopt do not wish to forbid others from doing so.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Political economy here points to heavy regulation coexisting with legal availability rather than outright bans — a compliance-cost regime, not a prohibition regime.
insights.locator: Most who would adopt still favor strict regulation

insights.claim: The paper's core framework is that when a technology promises large private benefits but imposes social costs markets do not price, observed demand does not reveal how citizens want that technology governed.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Strong consumer uptake is not a defense against regulation in these categories — use survey-based governance preferences, not sales curves, to forecast policy risk.
insights.quote: demand need not reveal how citizens want it governed
insights.locator: When a new technology promises large private benefits

insights.claim: The experiment randomized benefit domain, mechanism, heritability, purpose and risk across vignettes, then elicited stated adoption, preferred regulation, and ethical and societal concerns for each respondent's assigned vignette.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: The attribute-randomized design makes the framing and purpose effects causal rather than correlational, which raises the weight the findings deserve in policy forecasting.
insights.locator: The experiment randomizes benefit domain, mechanism, heritability

insights.claim: Productivity enhancement generates the most ethical concern of any attribute tested, yet attracts the least demanded regulation, and respondents favor subsidizing rather than taxing its adoption.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Cognitive/productivity enhancement may face public subsidy tailwinds rather than tax headwinds despite being the most morally contested use case — the opposite of the usual sin-tax playbook.
insights.quote: Productivity enhancement generates the most ethical concern of any attribute but attracts the least regulation
insights.locator: Productivity enhancement generates the most ethical concern

insights.claim: The pattern of wanting subsidies rather than taxes for productivity enhancement is read as reflecting a concern about access rather than about safety.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Equity-of-access, not harm, is the likely axis of political conflict over enhancement — watch for coverage-mandate and subsidy fights rather than safety bans.
insights.quote: consistent with a concern about access rather than safety
insights.locator: respondents favor subsidizing rather than taxing

insights.claim: Cowen singles out and repeats the productivity-enhancement finding, signalling he views moral resistance to productivity-boosting technology as the underappreciated result in the paper.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: If public ethical discomfort concentrates precisely on productivity gains, growth-enhancing technologies carry a legitimacy discount that valuation models rarely include.
insights.quote: And I will repeat this segment: “Productivity enhancement generates the most ethical concern of any attribute…”
insights.locator: And I will repeat this segment

themes.theme: Cowen's attack on the paper's conclusion

insights.claim: Cowen judges the authors' closing claim — that the demand/governance divergence gives regulators a basis to align the direction of technical change with societal values — to be completely unwarranted and a classic example of underidentified political bias in academic reasoning.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A reminder to separate the empirical result from the pro-regulation policy inference bolted onto it when reading academic work used to justify intervention.
insights.quote: the last sentence of the authors is completely unwarranted, and is a classic example of underidentified political bias in academic reasoning
insights.locator: Do note of course that the last sentence

insights.claim: The working paper is by Giovanni Immordino, Mario Macis, Immacolata Marino and Fabrizio Panebianco and is circulated through NBER.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Sourcing detail for anyone tracking the academic pipeline that feeds enhancement-technology regulation debates.
insights.locator: That is from a new NBER working paper
